```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The 90-day paying-customer constraint favors B. A has a hard gate before it can take money for its core product: IRS e-file Provider authorization, which the brief says (citing IRS Pub 3112) can take up to 45 days and requires fingerprinting and a suitability check. That consumes half the window before launch. B has no licensing gate. Its only stated review step is Stripe app marketplace review, and a first customer could be sold directly without a marketplace listing.",
    "B's failure mode is cheaper for a solo operator. A's brief says PFIC/FBAR/FATCA errors can cost customers tens of thousands of dollars, and a new one-person brand must win trust against incumbents with 100k to 165k users. B's worst case is a lost or delayed swag package and customs friction, which is operationally annoying but recoverable.",
    "B sells to a business and needs only one buyer to hit the goal. Willingness to pay is anchored by SwagUp's published $99 to $999/mo tiers. The brief cites founders (Endcrawl, BurnRate) describing the pain and the desire for welcome kits, so direct outreach to a handful of SaaS founders is a plausible path to one paying account within 90 days.",
    "Both ideas face entrenched incumbents offering the same core mechanic. A has six named competitors all serving the investor tier. B has SwagUp, Sendoso and Z-Swag already doing Stripe-triggered sends. Competition therefore does not separate them, and the decision falls to time-to-first-revenue and downside risk, where B is better.",
    "B's key weakness is lack of differentiation versus SwagUp's existing Stripe/Zapier flow. This threatens long-term defensibility more than it threatens landing a single first customer, for example with a done-for-you setup offer. A's barriers (authorization timing, liability, trust) block the first sale itself."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's demand evidence consists of three forum quotes about PFIC pain and remediation or attorney costs. None shows a US expat dissatisfied with existing $120 to $200 DIY tools or willing to switch to a new product. The '$50K' quote concerns tax liability and professional fees, not software. The 'underserved sub-segment' claim is therefore inferred from incumbents' upsell pricing, not evidenced. The community/forum acquisition channel likewise has no cost or conversion data, only the note that incumbents are already present there.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. A has the stronger organic demand evidence, independent forum posts versus B's vendor-published case studies. A's software-only nature also suits an AI-agent company better than B's physical fulfillment. The pick hinges on the 90-day constraint and the IRS authorization delay. If A pivoted to the narrower PFIC-calculation wedge raised in its open questions, which might avoid e-file authorization, the comparison could flip, but that option is unevidenced in the brief. B remains vulnerable to having no reason to exist beyond SwagUp plus Zapier, and its per-package economics for low-ACV SaaS are unresolved."
}
```
